first_draft.title: Alice, Bob, and the Missing Bell
first_draft.text:
Alice had a best friend with whiskers as long as paintbrushes and a tail that curled like a question mark. His name was Bob, and Bob was a cat.

Every morning, Bob wore a silver bell on a red ribbon around his neck. When he trotted across the kitchen floor, it went ding, ding, ding, like a tiny bird singing. Alice loved that sound more than almost anything.

One sunny Saturday, the bell was gone. Bob searched under the table. He searched behind the fridge. He even poked his nose into the sugar bowl, which made him sneeze. "Achoo!" said Bob, and Alice giggled.

"Don't worry, Bob," said Alice. "We'll find it together. Detectives always start with clues." She grabbed her notebook and a pencil with a chewed end. Bob wagged his tail very seriously, as if he were a detective too.

They tiptoed into the garden. The grass was tall and tickly. Alice checked the flowerpots. Bob checked the old shed, where a spider was busy weaving a web. "Excuse me, Mr. Spider," said Bob politely. The spider waved one leg and kept weaving. No bell was there. Alice wrote, Not in the shed.

They walked past the wobbly fence, the rain barrel, and the bird bath. Bob's nose twitched. "Ding?" he whispered hopefully. But the only sounds were a faraway dog barking and the rustle of leaves. Alice sat down on the back step and sighed. Bob sat beside her and leaned his warm side against her knee.

"Maybe it fell off when you chased that butterfly," Alice said softly. Bob closed his eyes and thought very hard. Then his ears popped up. He had heard something. Very faintly, from under the old wooden bench, came a tiny sound. Ding.

Alice dropped onto her tummy in the grass and peeked underneath. There, tangled in a clump of clover, sat the bell, shining in a patch of sunlight. Bob's eyes went round with joy. Then Alice frowned. The red ribbon was torn in two.

"Oh no," said Alice. Bob gave a small, worried mew. Alice tapped her chin. "Wait here," she said, and she ran inside. She came back with Grandma's sewing basket, a spool of red thread, and a pair of sharp, shiny scissors. Together, they tied the ribbon in a neat double knot. Bob shook his head, and the bell rang out. Ding, ding, ding.

Alice wrote one last line in her notebook: Case closed. Bob purred so loudly that the bell jingled along with him.

The sun slid behind the hill, and the sky turned the color of warm honey. Back in the kitchen, Alice and Bob curled up together on the soft rug beside the window. The clock ticked slowly. The house grew quiet.

"Ding," whispered Bob, very softly.

"Ding," whispered Alice.

Bob's tail rested over her toes. His purr grew slow and low. Alice's breathing grew slow too, and her eyes grew heavy.

Goodnight, Alice.

Goodnight, Bob.

Goodnight, little bell.

request: Leo and his dog Rocket go on a treasure hunt in the backyard

first_draft.title: Rocket and the Buried Treasure
first_draft.text:
Leo found the map folded inside an old rubber boot behind the garden shed. The paper was as yellow as butter and smelled of dust and pine needles. A wobbly black X sat beside a crooked oak tree, and across the top, in spidery letters, someone had written: TREASURE FOR A BRAVE CAPTAIN.

"Rocket, we're pirates now!" Leo whispered.

Rocket's tail thumped against the grass. Thump, thump, thump. Then he sniffed the map so hard that his whiskers tickled Leo's nose, and Leo giggled into his sleeve.

Leo tucked the map into his pocket and read the first clue out loud. "Three giant steps past the bird bath." He counted, one, two, three, and his sneakers squelched in the wet grass. "Now look under the thing that sleeps all day."

Rocket trotted straight to the wheelbarrow, which was tipped on its side, and barked. "Woof! Woof!"

Underneath was a small wooden box. Inside was a dry leaf, a chewed-up bottle cap, and a note that said, in tiny writing: Next, dig where the owl sleeps.

"Which owl?" Leo asked. He unfolded the map, and his heart sank. A puddle had smudged the bottom corner, and the ink had run into a blue blob. He could not tell which tree the clue meant.

Rocket dug at the skinny birch by the fence. Dirt flew everywhere, and a sock popped out of the hole.

"Rocket, not the birch!" Leo laughed, but he still felt stuck. He sat down on the back steps and chewed his lip. Rocket flopped beside him with a happy sigh and a sock still hanging from his mouth.

Then the kitchen light spilled through the window, warm and bright, right onto the map. Leo held it up. Faint pencil lines glowed through the paper. A tiny owl was drawn on a branch of the crooked oak, and next to it were the words: Under the hollow.

"Rocket! It's the oak!" Leo shouted, and he leaped off the steps.

They raced across the lawn. Leo looked up into the oak tree and saw a dark hole in the trunk, just above the roots. It was the owl's old home. He knelt down and began to dig with the garden trowel. Scritch, scratch. Rocket dug too, with his big paws flinging soil in all directions.

Clink!

Leo's trowel hit something hard. He scraped away the dirt and pulled out a dented metal tin, shiny with a little mud. The latch was stiff, but he wiggled it until it popped open with a click.

Inside were gold-foil coins, a shiny blue marble, and a folded note in his grandmother's loopy handwriting: To my brave captain, Leo. Share the coins with your first mate. Love, Gran.

Rocket's nose poked into the tin. Leo broke a crunchy dog biscuit shaped like a bone from the bottom of the tin, and Rocket gobbled it up in one happy gulp.

By the time they walked back to the house, the sky was turning the color of plums. Gran was waiting on the porch with a blanket and two mugs of warm cocoa. Leo wrapped himself up, and Rocket curled against his feet with a tired grunt.

The crickets began to sing. The porch light hummed, soft and low. Leo yawned, and the map slipped gently into his lap.

The night grew quiet. The stars came out, one by one.

Good night, little pirate.

first_draft.title: The Midnight Crunch Party
first_draft.text:
When the kitchen went dark and the fridge gave its sleepy hum, the vegetables began to wake up. Behind the cheese drawer, a tiny carrot named Pip stretched his curly green top and gave a happy wiggle. "Party time!" he whispered.

In the crisper drawer, the peas giggled, a beet rolled over with a squelchy sploosh, and a lettuce leaf fluffed herself up like a feather pillow. Tonight was the Midnight Crunch Party, and everyone knew the rule. The party could not start until the Silver Bell rang.

Pip hurried to the bell's shelf. It was empty. Only a sticky ring and a crumb of cheese sat where the bell should be.

"Where is it?" squeaked Pinky the radish, who was round and pink and always a little worried.

"Maybe it rolled under the butter," said Bramble the broccoli, bouncing her tree-top hair. Pip wiggled to the edge of the shelf and peeked down. Far below, between the milk jug and the butter dish, something glinted like a tiny moon.

"Heave-ho!" Pip pushed the milk jug with all his might. It only sloshed. Glug, glug, glug! Milk splashed everywhere, and the jug went flop onto its side.

Lettuce tried to float down like a leaf in the wind, but she was too floppy and landed on Pinky with a soft FLUMP. "Sorry, sorry!" she puffed.

Bramble tried swinging on her stalk, but it was too short. She bonked her head on a yogurt pot. "Ouch, my crunchy knees!" she groaned.

Pip sat down with a sigh. His curly top drooped. The bell was so close, and yet it might as well have been on the moon.

Then Pip heard the fridge humming, low and steady. Hmmmmm. He sat up straight. "Friends! Let's hum like the fridge!"

So they did. The peas hummed in high squeaks. Lettuce hummed in a soft, rustly voice. Bramble hummed so deeply that her leaves shivered. Pinky hummed with her eyes squeezed shut, and Pip hummed loudest of all. Mmmmm-mmmm-MMMMM!

The butter dish wobbled. It wiggled. It rocked, once, twice, and then, plink! Out popped the Silver Bell, spinning across the shelf like a coin.

"Catch it!" cried Pip.

Pinky rolled, round and bouncy, straight into the bell's path. Bonk! The bell tumbled into a nest of lettuce leaves, and Lettuce gave a happy wobble that caught it gently.

DING-A-LING! The sound rang out through the whole fridge.

The party began! The peas bounced like popcorn. The beet did the Squish-and-Splat, and Bramble danced the Broccoli Boogie with her leaves flapping. Pip spun in a circle until his top swirled. "Crunch-a-doodle! Snap-a-dee!" they all sang, and the cheese drawer snapped its own little tune in reply.

After a while, the dancing slowed. The bell gave one last soft ding. The fridge hummed more quietly now. Hmmmm... hmmm...

The peas yawned, one, two, three. The beet tucked itself into a corner. Lettuce spread her big leaves like a blanket, and Pinky snuggled up beside Pip, warm and round.

Pip's curly top flopped sideways. "Goodnight, crisper drawer," he whispered.

"Goodnight, Silver Bell," murmured Bramble, already drifting off.

The fridge hummed softly. Hmmmm. The light dimmed. The vegetables breathed slow and sleepy, and the kitchen was still.

Hush now, little veggies. The fridge is humming you to sleep.

Once upon a time, a goose named Gertrude lived on a farm beside a silver pond. Gertrude had the loudest honk in the whole wide world. HONK! It rattled the barn doors. It shook the apples off the trees.

"Hush now," snorted Pig. "SNURK! SNURK!" The hens woke up and flapped and squawked.

Gertrude hid behind a bale of hay. Her tail feathers poked out the side. Pig squealed, "I can see you!"

The sheep sighed. "Now I have to start all over again."

Gertrude's neck drooped low. "I only wanted to sing to the moon," she said. "It looks so lonely up there."

Splash! A small frog hopped onto a lily pad. He did not croak. He did not jump. He just sat very still and blinked at the moon.

"Do you like my song?" Gertrude asked. The frog blinked again, which seemed to mean yes.

Gertrude tiptoed to the water's edge. She tucked her long neck down low. She said, "Hmm... hmm..." very softly, like a bee in a blanket.

The frog blinked. The cow yawned. Snore, snore, went the pig, soft as a pillow. "Hmm... hmm..." sang Gertrude, soft as a feather.

Ripples danced on the pond. The moon smiled down. One by one, the animals curled up in the hay. Even the hens tucked their heads under their wings.

Gertrude folded her wings and tucked her head beside her feet. Hmm, hmm, went the goose, softer and softer, until the farm was quiet and the stars were sleepy too.

"I am a people-eating monster!" he boomed one blustery Tuesday, so loudly that the bridge rattled and a flock of starlings flapped away in a fright. "Hats, socks, mittens, kites. I shall gobble them all!"

Nell Button heard the boom from her kitchen. She was seven years old, with a brave heart and a nose that was always cold. Her little brother Pip had been playing by the bridge that morning, and now his red woolly hat was missing.

"Gobbleton ate it," Pip whispered, his eyes as round as buttons. "I saw his teeth. They go all the way around."

Mum put down her tea towel and wound a scarf around her neck. "Let's go and see," she said. "Monsters are often just hungry, and hungry things are easier to talk to after a snack."

While Nell and Pip pulled on their boots, Mum baked a tray of blueberry muffins. The kitchen smelled of warm butter and cinnamon. Pip held a muffin in one mitten and Nell's hand in the other all the way down the lane.

At the bridge, the river gurgled and the reeds whispered. Gobbleton sat in the middle of the stones, picking a sock out of his left horn.

"Excuse me," said Nell politely. "Did you eat my brother's hat?"

Gobbleton lifted his enormous head. "Eat? I am a people-eating monster. Hats are only the appetizer. Now run along before I get peckish."

Pip hid behind Nell's coat. Nell took a deep breath. "Peckish is a funny word," she said. "Are you very hungry?"

"Hungry!" Gobbleton groaned, and his belly rumbled like a thunder cloud with a tummy ache. "I have eaten every mitten in the village, and still my tummy grumbles."

Mum set the basket down on the stones. "Perhaps you have been eating the wrong things," she said. "Have you tried a muffin?"

Gobbleton gobbled the first muffin in one enormous gulp. Then he gobbled the second, and the third, and the fourth, until the basket was empty and his belly was as round as a pumpkin. He burped a tiny cloud of cinnamon.

"Still hungry," he sighed, and his horns drooped.

"You are gobbling so fast that you forget to taste," said Nell. "Try slowly."

Gobbleton picked up one more muffin. He sniffed it. He closed his eyes. He nibbled one tiny corner, then another. "Mmm," he hummed, very softly. "Warm. Sweet. Crumbly."

Then his big green face crinkled, and he looked down at the water. "I took the hat because it was soft and warm," he mumbled. "Everyone drops things by my bridge, and nobody ever stops to say hello. Except you."

Nell sat down on the cold stone beside him. She broke a muffin in half and held one piece up. "Then have some with us," she said.

Gobbleton's huge nostrils quivered. He took the piece as gently as a bird takes a crumb. Pip crept out from behind the coat and offered him the very last muffin in his mitten. Gobbleton blinked, then smiled a smile that went all the way up to his horns.

"HIC!"

Out shot the red woolly hat, like a cork from a bottle. It sailed through the air and landed right on top of Pip's head.

Pip giggled so hard he almost fell into the river. "It fits!" he cried.

"Hats belong on heads," said Mum, laughing, "and muffins belong in tummies."

Gobbleton hung his head sheepishly. "Next time, I shall ask first," he promised, in a voice as soft as moss.

The sun slipped behind the hills, and the sky turned the color of plums. The river began to hum a slow, sleepy song. Pip yawned a yawn so big that his hat wobbled.

As they walked home, Gobbleton waved one long green arm from the bridge. Nell waved back. Pip's eyelids drooped. Mum carried the empty basket and smiled.

At home, the lamp glowed warm and yellow. Nell tucked the quilt up under Pip's chin and kissed his hat-flattened hair.

"Goodnight, river," she whispered. "Goodnight, hungry monster. Goodnight, muffins."

first_draft.text:
The house on Hollow Lane had been quiet for three whole nights, and then the attic began to groan.

"Ooooooh," said the attic. "Ooooh, woe. Woe."

Ethan pulled his blanket up to his nose. His sister Lily pulled hers up to her eyes. "That's just the pipes," Ethan whispered, although pipes do not usually say woe.

A clank rolled down the stairs like a bowling ball. Then came a long, wobbly wail that made the window rattle in its frame.

"Ethan," Lily whispered. "Are we going up there?"

"Are you?"

"Only if you go first."

So they crept up the creaky attic stairs, one step at a time. Ethan's flashlight shook so hard that its beam danced across the rafters like a moth. Dust tickled their noses. In the far corner, under a heap of old sheets, something was shivering and sniffling.

"Oooo," moaned the heap. "Ooo... ah... ah... AH-CHOOOO!"

The sheets flew up. A pale, wispy ghost popped out, wearing a pointed hat and a very red nose.

"Oh, good gracious," said the ghost, dabbing his nose with a sock. "I was going to be terrifying. Now I'm just a snuffle."

Lily giggled before she could stop herself. Ethan let out a squeak of a laugh, and then he clapped a hand over his mouth.

"Who are you?" he asked.

"I am Mortimer Moan, haunter of Hollow House for two hundred years," said the ghost. "I have a cold. A ghost with a cold can only hiccup and squeak. And tonight is the Midnight Moaning Gala, and they will never let me in if I sound like a teakettle."

"Why are you under the sheets?" asked Lily.

Mortimer sighed, and his glow flickered like a candle. "I tried to float down the chimney to practice my wail. Instead, my sheet caught on that nail behind the trunk. Now I am stuck, and every time I wiggle, I sneeze."

Ethan shone his flashlight on the trunk. Sure enough, a long white corner of sheet hung from a rusty nail, fluttering like a flag.

Lily grabbed one end and pulled. The sheet stretched with a long, sad "eeeeek." Mortimer yelped, then sneezed so hard that his hat spun off and landed on Ethan's head.

"Stop, stop!" said Ethan. He pushed the hat back onto the ghost, gently. "Pulling makes it tighter. We need to slide it off, slow and easy, like untangling a kite string."

So Ethan held the sheet near the nail. Lily wiggled the cloth sideways, one tiny inch at a time. Mortimer hummed a soft, rumbly note while they worked, and the hum made the dust sparkle in the flashlight beam.

"Ooo... mmm," hummed Mortimer. "Hmm... that's better."

With one last gentle tug, the sheet slid free. Mortimer floated up, twirled once, and bowed.

"Thank you," he said. "Now, I believe you two need a warm drink, and so do I."

Downstairs, Grandma was already waiting, humming by the kettle. She poured warm milk with honey for the children and a spoonful of honey in a cup for Mortimer, who sipped it through his sock.

"Mmm," he said, and this time the sound came out as a soft, round hum that made the cups tremble. "Ooooo, that's a moan I can be proud of."

Lily yawned. Ethan yawned too.

Upstairs, the attic floorboards gave one last creak, and then a soft, sleepy hum drifted down through the house.

The lamps dimmed. The blankets grew warm. Somewhere in the attic, a ghost with a cold was fast asleep.

Goodnight, Hollow House. Goodnight, Ethan. Goodnight, Lily.

first_draft.text:
On a hill above the village of Nettlewick, where the sheep wore tiny bells, lived a knight named Sir Wendell. He had a shiny helmet, a round shield, and a sword that hummed whenever he polished it.

One windy evening, a sound came rolling up the hill. AH-CHOO! It was so loud that the windows rattled, the gate creaked, and three sleepy crows tumbled off the fence.

Sir Wendell buckled on his boots and rode down to the old stone bridge. Under the arch sat a dragon no bigger than a wheelbarrow. Her name was Pepper, and her nose was as pink as a ripe plum.

"Good evening," said Sir Wendell politely. "Are you unwell?"

"I have a tickle," sniffed Pepper. "It starts in my nose and goes all the way to my tail. Every time it comes, I sneeze, and every sneeze blows out the lanterns in the village. Now the bakers cannot see their dough, and the cat thinks it is midnight."

Sir Wendell rubbed his chin. "Then we must find the tickle."

First, he tried his feathered plume. He wiggled it under Pepper's nose. She giggled. "Hee... hee... AH-CHOO!" The plume flew over the hedge, and three more lanterns blinked out with a soft pop.

Next, he poured warm ginger tea into a tin cup. Pepper sipped it with both claws. "Mmm, spicy," she said. Then her eyes went wide. "Ahh... ahh... AH-CHOO!" The cup spun into the river with a splash, and the whole village went dark.

Sir Wendell sat down on the cold stone. Pepper sniffled, and a fat tear rolled down her scales. "I am sorry, Sir," she whispered. "I only wanted to help the bakers."

Sir Wendell watched the wind ripple across the water. "Pepper, when did the tickle start?"

"This afternoon," she said. "I flew low over the meadow and went right through the dandelions."

"Aha," said Sir Wendell, and his sword gave a happy hum. "Hold very still. Let me look."

He held up his lantern, the one that had not gone out, and peered into her nose. Caught in the tiny hairs was a single dandelion seed, fluffy and silver as a moonbeam.

"Hold still, Pepper, that's it," he murmured. He lifted the seed with a soft cloth, slow and gentle, the way you lift a bee off a flower. Pepper's eyes crossed. Her whiskers quivered. "Ahhhh... ahhhhh..."

"Ahhh-CHOO!" The seed shot out, floated up over the bridge, and drifted away like a little star. Pepper sighed. "Oh. Oh, that is much better."

Across the valley, the lanterns of Nettlewick began to glow again, one by one, as the villagers relit them. The baker waved his floury hat. Sir Wendell waved back.

"Thank you, Sir Wendell," said Pepper. "You were not one bit fierce, but you were very kind."

Sir Wendell laughed and wrapped his cloak around her warm, rumbly shoulders.

The bridge creaked softly. The river murmured its old song. Pepper gave a long, slow yawn and curled up like a sleepy cat. Sir Wendell sat beside her, humming a quiet tune until the stars came out, one by one.

"Goodnight, Pepper," he whispered.

"Goodnight, Sir Wendell," she whispered back, and the valley grew still.

first_draft.title: Maya's Hop, Skip, Hello
first_draft.text:
On Sunday night, Maya sat on the edge of her bed and swung her feet. Her new backpack hung on the doorknob, stiff and shiny and waiting. Tomorrow was Monday. Tomorrow was a brand-new school.

"What if nobody wants to be my friend?" she whispered.

Mama sat down beside her. The bed gave a soft creak. Mama smelled like warm bread and lavender soap. "New places feel wobbly for everybody," she said. "Even grown-ups. Want to practice?"

"Practice what?"

"Our secret hello. Hop, skip, hello!"

Maya giggled. She hopped off the bed on one foot, skipped twice across the rug, and said, "Hello!" in a squeaky voice. Mama laughed so hard her glasses slid down her nose.

"Hop, skip, hello," Maya whispered, snuggling under her quilt. "Hop, skip, hello."

On Monday morning, the classroom smelled like crayons and wet paint. Maya's sneakers squeaked across the shiny floor. Her tummy went flip, flop, flip.

Her teacher, Ms. Lin, smiled. "Everyone, this is Maya. Let's find a seat." Maya sat at the end of a table. Three children were building a tower of blocks.

The tower was tall and wobbly. A boy with a red hat stacked block after block, and he never once looked up. Maya opened her mouth. Nothing came out but a tiny squeak.

Her shoulders drooped. She picked up a crayon and drew a sad little cloud in the corner of her paper. Then she drew another one. Two sad clouds, sitting in the rain.

At lunch, Maya sat with her lunchbox on her knees. Across the room, a girl with two long braids sat all alone. She stared at her sandwich and nibbled her crust very slowly. Maya knew that look.

Maya took a big breath. Hop, skip, hello. She hopped, and her lunchbox bounced. She skipped, and her juice box went boing against her leg.

"Hello," she said.

The girl blinked. Then she giggled. "Hello. I'm Priya. Did you just hop?"

"Hop, skip, hello," said Maya. "It's my secret."

Priya hopped too, a tiny hop, and laughed. Then the boy with the red hat wandered over, holding his sandwich. "What's the hop?" he asked.

"Hop, skip, hello!" Maya and Priya shouted together.

He hopped so high his hat tumbled off. Everybody laughed, and the lunchroom bubbled with giggles like popping soap. "I'm Theo," he said, grinning, and he picked up his hat.

At recess, the three of them hopped in a wiggly line across the playground. Theo hopped the highest. Priya skipped the fastest. Maya skipped and hopped and squeaked, and nobody minded one bit.

That night, Maya lay in bed with her backpack by the door. The room was dark and quiet. Her quilt was warm and heavy, like a big soft hug.

"Hop, skip, hello," she whispered.

Mama's footsteps padded down the hall, soft as a mouse. The hall light glowed yellow under the door. Maya's eyes grew heavy.

Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Theo.

Goodnight, Maya.

final.title: Maya's Hop, Skip, Hello
final.text:
On Sunday night, Maya sat on the edge of her bed. She swung her feet back and forth. Her new backpack hung on the doorknob. It was stiff and shiny and waiting. Tomorrow was Monday. Tomorrow was a brand-new school.

"What if nobody wants to be my friend?" she whispered.

Mama sat down beside her. The bed gave a soft creak. Mama smelled like warm bread and lavender soap. "New places feel wobbly for everybody," she said. "Even grown-ups. Want to practice?"

"Practice what?"

"Our secret hello. Hop, skip, hello!"

Maya giggled. She hopped off the bed on one foot. She skipped twice across the rug. "Hello!" she said, in a squeaky voice. Mama laughed so hard her glasses slid down her nose.

"Hop, skip, hello," Maya whispered, snuggling under her quilt. "Hop, skip, hello."

On Monday morning, the classroom smelled like crayons and wet paint. Maya's sneakers squeaked on the shiny floor. Her tummy went flip, flop, flip.

Her teacher, Ms. Lin, smiled. "Everyone, this is Maya. Let's find you a seat." Sunflowers nodded at the big window. In the reading corner, a fat picture book sat on a cushion. Maya sat at the end of a table. Three children were building a tower of blocks.

The tower was tall and wobbly. A boy with a red hat stacked block after block. He never once looked up. He hummed a little song to himself, hmm, hmm, hmm. Maya opened her mouth. Nothing came out but a tiny squeak.

Her shoulders drooped. She picked up a crayon and drew a sad little cloud in the corner of her paper. Then she drew another one. Two sad clouds, sitting in the rain.

At lunch, Maya sat with her lunchbox on her knees. Across the room, a girl with two long braids sat all alone. She stared at her sandwich. She nibbled her crust very slowly. Maya knew that look. It was the look she had felt all morning.

Maya took a big breath. Hop, skip, hello. She hopped, and her lunchbox bounced. She skipped, and her juice box went boing against her leg.

"Hello," she said.

The girl blinked. Then she giggled. "Hello. I'm Priya. Did you just hop?"

"Hop, skip, hello," said Maya. "It's my secret."

Priya hopped too, a tiny hop, and laughed. Then the boy with the red hat wandered over. He held his sandwich in one hand. "What's the hop?" he asked.

"Hop, skip, hello!" Maya and Priya shouted together.

He hopped so high that his hat tumbled off. Everybody laughed. The lunchroom bubbled with giggles, like popping soap. "I'm Theo," he said, grinning. He picked up his hat and put it back on, backward.

At recess, the three of them hopped in a wiggly line across the playground. Theo hopped the highest. Priya skipped the fastest. Maya skipped and hopped and squeaked. Their sneakers went slap, slap, slap on the blacktop. Nobody minded one bit.

That night, Maya lay in bed. Her backpack waited by the door. The room was dark and quiet. Her quilt was warm and heavy, like a big soft hug.

"Hop, skip, hello," she whispered.

Mama's footsteps padded down the hall, soft as a mouse. The hall light glowed yellow under the door. Tomorrow, the sunflowers would be waiting in the window. Maya's eyes grew heavy.

Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Theo.

Goodnight, Maya.

first_draft.title: The Bell by the Back Door
first_draft.text:
The kitchen was too quiet. Sam sat on the bottom step with his chin in his hands, listening for a sound that wasn't there. For eight years, every evening had come with a jingle from the back door, where Biscuit always wagged his way in, slow and grey around the muzzle, his tail thumping like a drum. Last week, Biscuit grew tired and went to sleep for the very last time. Now the house felt like it was still waiting for him.

Mom sat down beside him and rubbed his back. "I have an idea," she said. "Would you like to hang Biscuit's bell on his old hook?" Sam nodded. The little brass bell had hung from Biscuit's collar, and it had always chimed when he trotted past. Sam wanted that sound back, even just once. But when they reached the hook by the back door, it was empty.

"Where could it be?" Sam asked. He checked his coat pockets. He checked the shoe basket, where a squeaky rubber duck was hiding behind the boots. "Boof!" barked Dad from the doorway, wagging his hand like a tail. Sam giggled so hard he almost hiccupped. Then his smile wobbled, and he pressed his face into Dad's sleeve. "I miss him," he said. "I know, buddy. Me too."

Sam wiped his eyes and thought hard, the way Biscuit used to think about where the best crumbs had fallen. Where did Biscuit like to nap? Not on the cold tiles. Not in the sunny patch by the window. Sam pulled on his slippers and tiptoed out to the porch, where the wooden swing creaked softly in the cool air. Under the faded blue cushion, something glinted. It was a small brass bell, tangled in a loop of old wool blanket, with a tiny tooth mark on one side.

Sam held the bell in his palm. It was cold at first, then warm from his hand. He gave it a gentle shake. Ting. It sounded softer than he remembered, but it was the same bell. Sam felt sad and happy at the same time, like a rainy day with a rainbow in it. He carried it inside with both hands, careful not to let it ring too loudly.

Dad lifted him up, and Sam hung the bell on the hook. It swayed, and then it gave one small, sweet jingle. "Night, Biscuit," Sam whispered. Dad squeezed his shoulder. Mom turned off the big light and left on the little lamp.

Upstairs, Sam pulled his blanket up to his chin and listened. Down below, the bell gave one more soft tinkle as a breeze slipped through the window. The house was no longer quiet, only calm. Outside, the moon climbed over the garden, and the grass lay silver and still. Sam's eyes grew heavy. Tinkle. Hush. Goodnight, Biscuit. Goodnight, Sam.

“Whoo-whoo, I am so sleepy,” she said. “But where is my blanket?”

Olive’s blanket was made of soft gray moss. Every night it wrapped around her like a hug. Tonight, it was gone.

Olive yawned so wide that a feather drifted down. “Whoo, whoo,” she mumbled. “Blanket, where are you?”

She looked under the leaves. She peeked behind a pinecone. She tapped the bark with her beak. Tap, tap, tap. Nothing answered but a sleepy cricket: chirp... chirp...

A tiny brown mouse peeked out from a log. “Hello, Olive,” she squeaked. “I saw something soft float over the pond, all fluffy and gray.”

Olive flapped her wings, slow and quiet. Whoosh, whoosh. She glided over the pond, where moonlight silvered the water and frogs croaked low and sleepy. Cool air tickled her feathers.

There, in a bramble bush, hung her blanket, tangled in thorny twigs. Olive tugged. Crackle! The twigs poked her feathers. “Oh my,” she sighed.

Olive stopped tugging. She took a slow breath and hummed, hmmm, hmmm, the way her mother used to. Then she picked at one twig at a time, gently, gently, until the blanket slid free.

“You did it!” cheered Mouse from the grass.

Olive thanked her with a soft hoot, and Mouse giggled. Then she flew up, up, past the tallest branches, her wings light as dandelion fluff, back to her cozy tree.

She wrapped the moss around her shoulders. It smelled of rain and pine. It felt warm and heavy, just right, like a sleepy sigh. The wind hummed a lullaby through the branches, and Olive hummed along, softer and slower each time.

Stars blinked, one, two, three. Frogs yawned. Mouse curled up in her log, and the cricket went quiet.

Olive’s eyes drifted closed. Hmmm, hmmm... whoo... shh... goodnight.

first_draft.title: Pebble and the Rainbow Room
first_draft.text:
Zoe had a pocket full of crystals and a tortoise named Pebble, who walked as slowly as a sleepy Sunday. On the last warm afternoon of summer, they climbed the grassy hill behind Grandpa's cottage until they reached a crack in the rock. A cool breeze drifted out of it. It smelled of wet stones and violets after rain.

"Are you brave?" Zoe whispered. Pebble blinked his wrinkly eyes and took one slow step forward. "Good. Me too. Mostly."

She clicked on her torch. A yellow circle slid across the walls. Somewhere far away, water dripped, plip, plop, like a tiny drum keeping time.

The tunnel twisted left, then right, then left again. Zoe trailed her fingers along the rock, which felt bumpy and cold, like the knuckles of a giant. Pebble's shell went tock, tock, tock against the stones.

"Slow and steady," Zoe said, which was exactly what Grandpa always said. She giggled, and the giggle bounced off the walls and came back to her, a little squeaky and a little silly.

Then the tunnel opened into a round room, and Zoe forgot how to breathe.

Crystals grew everywhere. Some were purple as ripe plums. Some were pale as milk. One tall crystal stood in the middle like a rocket waiting to launch. When the torchlight touched it, the whole room burst into colour. Rainbows skipped across the ceiling and danced over Pebble's shell and up Zoe's arms.

"Pebble," she breathed. "Look at this. Look!"

Pebble looked, very slowly, and then he made a small, happy sound, the kind a kettle makes just before it sings.

Zoe crouched beside the tallest crystal. Its surface was smooth as glass, but along one side ran a thin pink crack. Inside the crack, a little shard of crystal lay loose, glittering like a boiled sweet. Zoe's heart thumped. Her collection at home had nothing so beautiful. She reached out her hand.

Then she stopped.

"It's only a tiny piece," she whispered.

Pebble stretched out his neck and bumped her hand gently with his nose. Then he turned his head and looked at her with his sleepy, patient eyes.

Zoe thought about the dripping water that had made this room over more years than she could count. She thought about the other children in the village who might one day climb this hill and find the rainbow room. If the shard went into her pocket, the room would be a little less whole.

"Maybe this room belongs to everyone," she said. "Even you, Pebble."

Pebble yawned, which Zoe decided meant yes.

She drew her hand back and picked up the shard with two fingers. It was jagged along one edge. She turned it over, and then she noticed something. The crack in the big crystal had a matching notch, as if it had been waiting for this exact piece. Zoe held her breath and slid the shard into place.

Click.

The crystal hummed a low note, like a cello being played very softly, and the rainbows swirled brighter than before.

Zoe grinned so widely her cheeks hurt. She had put it back, and the room was whole again.

Then a stone clattered somewhere behind them. Zoe's heart jumped, and her torch wobbled. Pebble tucked his head into his shell and went very still. Zoe counted five slow breaths, until she heard only the drip, plip, plop once more.

"Just a loose stone," she said. Pebble poked his head back out, looking rather grumpy about the noise.

They crept back through the twisting tunnel, tock, tock, tock, and Zoe kept saying "slow and steady" under her breath. At last, a patch of gold light spilled through the crack. Grandpa stood at the entrance with his coat buttoned up to his chin and a flask of hot chocolate steaming in his hands.

"There you are!" he said. "I was just about to come in after you with a torch the size of a lamp post."

"Grandpa, I found the most amazing room," Zoe said, bouncing on her toes. "It's full of crystals that make rainbows. Pebble liked it too."

Pebble bumped against Grandpa's boot, as if to agree.

Grandpa listened to every word. Then he asked, "Did you take anything?"

Zoe looked at her empty hand, and then at her grandfather. She told him about the shard, and how she had almost kept it.

Grandpa's eyes crinkled at the corners. "I'm proud of you for choosing the right thing," he said. "Those crystals took longer to grow than these hills have been standing. Next weekend, we'll come back with a proper map and a guide from the museum, and you can show me everything."

"Really?" Zoe asked.

"Really," said Grandpa, and he poured her a cup of cocoa that tasted of cinnamon and warm kitchens.

That evening, Zoe sat in bed with Pebble snoring softly in his box by the window. She held the small clear crystal that Grandpa had found near the cave entrance, a chip that had broken off long ago and rolled into the grass for anyone to find. It felt cool at first, then slowly warm in her palm.

"Grandpa," she murmured, "I think the best treasures are the ones we share."

He smiled from the doorway. "That's right, sweetheart. And some treasures are best left right where they are."

He switched off the big light, leaving only the soft glow of the landing lamp. Outside, the breeze had gone still. The hill was quiet, and the stars were coming out one by one.

Zoe's eyes grew heavy. She tucked the crystal beside her pillow, where it caught the moonlight and glowed, just a little, like a secret kept safe.

"Goodnight, Pebble," she whispered. "Goodnight, hill."

Her eyelids fluttered shut.

"Goodnight, rainbow room."
